TESTIMONY IN SUPPORT OF
L.D. 181
AN ACT TO MODIFY THE CALCULATION OF PUPIL COUNTS USED FOR DETERMINATION OF
SCHOOL ADMINISTRATIVE UNIT OPERATING COSTS
February 26, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan Murphy and members of the Education and Cultural Affairs
Committee, I am Robbie Feinberg, the director of communications and government relations for Maine
School Management Association, speaking on behalf of the legislative committees of the Maine School
Boards Association and Maine School Superintendents Association in strong support of L.D. 181, An Act to
Modify the Calculation of Pupil Counts Used for Determination of School Administrative Unit Operating
Costs.
This policy is nearly identical to an amended bill crafted by the previous Legislature's Education Committee. It was crafted in a bipartisan manner, received a unanimous committee vote in support, passed the House and Senate, and only died because it was caught up in the chaos of the final few days of the session.
We are glad that Rep. Tuell has introduced this measure again. We believe it would provide more financial
stability to our local school districts, and we urge you to support it.
Fluctuating enrollment is a constant issue for our schools. In determining the amount of state funding a district will receive, the state's school funding formula looks at "the average of the pupil counts for October 1st of the 2 most recent calendar years." Our school leaders feel this approach is not sufficient at responding to changing student enrollment and adequately meeting student needs.
Many districts -- particularly those in smaller, more rural areas, may experience a large enrollment drop from
one year to the next, resulting in a decrease in state support. To preserve programming and staff, these districts must turn to their local taxpayers to make up the difference.
Other districts, meanwhile, have seen substantial enrollment increases. More students need support. But these
districts think the current, two-year averaged count doesn't get funding to these students quickly enough.
This bill proposes a solution that we think would support districts in both of these circumstances. By allowing a district to use the greater of its latest October 1" enrollment count, or the average count of the three most
recent calendar years, districts would be partially insulated from the financial impacts of a sudden, rapid drop in enrollment, while also more quickly receiving state support if they see more students.
We know that school funding can vary from year to year, and this bill would offer schools a level of financial assurance and stability. We view it as a positive step, and we hope you support it.

Steven W. Bailey MSBA Executive Director

Eileen E. King MSSA Executive Director

184253:
Testimony for
The Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
February 26, 2025
To: Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and other Distinguished Members of the
Education and Cultural Affairs Committee
From: Scott K. Porter, Superintendent of Schools, AOS 96 (11 Towns in the Machias Area) LD 181: "An Act to Modify the Calculation of Pupil Counts Used for Determination of
School Administrative Unit Operating Costs" .
As you know, the Essential Programs and Services Funding model is based on a variety of factors which includes student enrollment. The current Funding Formula averages two October
student counts to calculate an operating allocation on page 2 of the ED 279 Report. This bill
would change the operating calculation to an average of three October student counts or the most recent October student count, Whichever is greater. This would help districts with declining
enrollment, but would reward districts that have a one year enrollment increase. It is my hope
this Committee will support this method of calculating student counts in the EPS Funding
Formula.
Thank you.
10033329:
Val Caruso Augusta LD 181
Valerie Caruso As a professional educator for over 30 years, I have seen the impact of school districts that face annual challenges in passing budgets to fully fund local education. This should not happen and changes in funding must be proactively implemented. The way Maine calculates pupil counts plays a crucial role in determining funding for MSADs . However, the current formula does not always reflect the true financial needs of schools, especially those with fluctuating enrollments, high numbers of students requiring additional support, or rural districts facing unique challenges. To ensure fair and adequate funding, Maine should modify the calculation of pupil counts to better reflect the actual costs of educating students.
First, the current method of counting students does not fully account for those who require additional resources. For example, students with special needs, English language learners, and economically disadvantaged students often require extra support services, such as specialized instruction, counseling, and transportation. Simply counting all students equally ignores these added costs. A weighted funding system--where students with greater needs count more toward the total--would provide a more accurate reflection of each district's financial burden.
Additionally, fluctuating enrollments create budgeting challenges for many districts. Schools with declining populations may lose funding under the current system, even though many of their operating costs (such as building maintenance and staff salaries) remain fixed. Likewise, districts experiencing rapid growth may struggle to accommodate new students without immediate funding adjustments. A more flexible formula that considers multi-year enrollment trends or guarantees baseline funding levels would help districts plan more effectively.
Some may argue that altering the pupil count calculation could complicate the funding process or create disparities between districts. However, the goal should be equity, not just simplicity. By refining the way Maine counts students for funding purposes, the state can ensure that resources are allocated based on actual need, not just raw enrollment numbers.
In conclusion, Maine must modify its pupil count formula to reflect the real costs of educating students. A weighted funding system and adjustments for enrollment fluctuations would provide a fairer, more sustainable approach to school funding. Investing in an accurate and equitable funding model will ultimately lead to stronger schools and better outcomes for all students.

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, Distinguished Members of the
Education and Cultural Affairs Committee:
My name is Will Tuell. l represent House District 10 in central Washington County, and am here today to enthusiastically present LD 181, "An Act to Modify
the Calculation of Pupil Counts` Used for the Determination of School
'
Administrative Unit Operating Costs."
That's a mouthful, but for those of you who have been around the committee a couple of years, it should sound familiar. My predecessor, Hon. Ken "Bucket"
Davis, submitted this legislation at the request of our local school superintendent in the 131$` Legislature to ensure that rural, economically disadvantaged schools
were getting the funding they are supposed to under state law.
This committee came to a unanimous agreement, that bill, LD 808 sailed to passage, and was even voted off the special appropriations table in the last days
of the last session before it got caught up in a stack of bills the Chief Executive pocket vetoed.
l do not say that to point the finger, just to remind folks of the extraordinary effort this committee and the Legislature put fon/vard to pass a quality piece of
legislation, and to explain why it is back before you today.
Despite the long and confusing title, LD 181 is really quite simple. lt funds
schools the greater of the average per pupil count over the last three years or the most recent October 1 count so that schools in rural areas which have seen
enrollment swings and those who have suddenly seen an influx of new students are made whole.
There are others behind me who will go much deeper into the weeds, and probably simplify this even further, but basically, DOE requires schools to report
enrollment numbers every October. Those enrollment figures are at the heart of the subsidy disbursement. But what happens when you have a student move into a community a week later, a month later, or for some crazy reason in the middle
of the coldest winter in ten years.
l

House District 10

lt happens, and in small, rural schools like ours in central Washington County
where budgets are bare bones, it means the school is educating a student - as they should - with no expectation of getting subsidy for that student until the
following year.
Mind you, that same student's family may move again before the school year is
out, leaving the local community where the student attended school, assuming the cost of the education and the possibility of never recouping subsidy.
There are as many reasons why students move as there are students. Whether
it's the housing crisis, drug crisis, foster care, family breakups, or the parents
discover that Maine is great in the summertime but living here full time in the coldest winter in a decade really isn't for them. There are a zillion reasons, but the bottom line is, our schools should not be left holding the bag.
That is why l believe this committee came up with a compromise that could work for school districts large and small. You will hear from some of those folks today
and their unique circumstances that could lead to funding going into areas that truly need it the most. ls this bill the answer to all our school funding problems? No, it isn't, but with
enrollment all over the place, it is more important than ever that the money does in fact follow the student and that those communities who are educating students "for free" are getting a measure of their expenses back.
As I said above, others behind me with the nuts and bolts knowledge of school
finance and enrollment will be testifying behind me, and will be in a much better position to answer any questions you may have. l would encourage you to take advantage of that opportunity, and move ahead with another unanimous vote of LD 181. Thank you.
House District 10
